questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how federal disputes are resolved
questions.stem: While drafting the survey protocol, Ana notes that the national park authority and the regional council each legislate on their own lands and that a supreme court settles conflicts between them.

options.text: A federal structure, because each level holds powers protected against the other.
A unitary structure, because the supreme court sits above both authorities.
options.misconception: assumes a single court makes the state unitary

options.text: A confederal structure, because the regional council keeps its own identity.
options.misconception: reads regional identity as evidence of confederation

options.text: A hybrid regime, because two institutions dispute the same ground.
options.misconception: confuses institutional rivalry with regime unfairness

questions.explanation: Protected powers at two levels, with disputes resolved by a court, mark a federal structure. A single court does not make a state unitary, and institutional rivalry says nothing about electoral fairness.
questions.hint: Check which level holds protected powers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a regime from its electoral features

stimulus.body: The station log records that polling stations open on schedule and that two opposition candidates filed nominations, although one withdrew after a visit from the regional office. Results are published two days later in a newspaper owned by a party member. The log notes that the previous election was contested by five parties.

questions.stem: Using the station log as evidence, which classification best fits the political system it describes?

options.text: A democratic regime, because elections are held on a fixed schedule.
options.misconception: treats a regular electoral calendar as sufficient

options.text: A hybrid regime, since competition is real but conditions are tilted.
An authoritarian regime, because a candidate withdrew under pressure.
options.misconception: converts one pressured withdrawal into full authoritarianism

options.text: A unitary state, because the regional office can influence elections.
options.misconception: confuses administrative hierarchy with regime classification

questions.explanation: Several candidates stand and results are published, so competition is real, but a pressured withdrawal and partisan ownership of results point to systematic unfairness, the hybrid pattern.
questions.hint: Weigh competition against tilt.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the features of a mixed system
questions.stem: Ana reports that the survey country has a directly elected president with a fixed term and a prime minister who can be removed by the legislature.

options.text: It is a presidential system, because the president is elected directly.
options.misconception: treats one elected office as proof of a presidential system

options.text: It is a parliamentary system, because the prime minister can be dismissed.
options.misconception: treats one confidence rule as proof of a parliamentary system

options.text: It is a mixed system, because it combines both executive designs.
It is a hybrid regime, because its elections are unfair.
options.misconception: uses the regime label without any evidence of unfairness

questions.explanation: A fixed-term elected president and a confidence-dependent prime minister are the two classic executive designs together. Mixing them describes institutional form, while the hybrid label is reserved for unfair elections.
questions.hint: Separate institutional form from electoral fairness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the confidence rule to government stability
questions.stem: Ana must explain to the survey team why a government can fall even when its successor would come from the same parliamentary majority.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that the confidence rule links the survival of a government to the continued willingness of the legislature to tolerate it, not simply to a fixed arithmetic majority at the moment of the election. A cabinet may lose that tolerance through scandal, defeat on a vote or a dispute over a budget, and once confidence fails the government must resign or seek a fresh mandate. Because the arithmetic of the chamber rarely changes between elections, a confidence crisis can remove a government whose seat count would have carried it through the next vote.

questions.explanation: The confidence rule tests continuing legislative tolerance, not a fixed seat count. A government can fall on a confidence vote even when its numbers would win the next election.
questions.hint: Confidence is about tolerance, not arithmetic.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read party counts against seat totals under proportionality
questions.stem: In the results table for the survey region, four parties hold seats and the largest holds thirty-eight of one hundred seats after polling forty percent of the vote.

options.text: The seat count is proportional, since forty of one hundred seats match forty percent of votes.
The seat count is disproportional, because the largest party did not win a majority.
options.misconception: reads proportionality as if it required a majority

options.text: The seat count is disproportional, because four parties shared all the seats.
options.misconception: treats the number of parties as evidence of distortion

options.text: The largest party is over-represented, because forty percent of votes is not a majority.
options.misconception: confuses proportionality with the need for a majority

questions.explanation: Proportional allocation delivers seats in the same proportion as votes, so forty percent of the vote yielding forty of one hundred seats is proportional. Proportionality is not the same thing as winning a majority.
questions.hint: Compare vote share with seat share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish federal from unitary authority
questions.stem: Reporting from the survey country, Noor observes that a single national law applies identically in every province and that provinces may be abolished by ordinary legislation.

options.text: A federal structure, since the law applies uniformly across all provinces.
options.misconception: confuses uniform law with constitutionally protected subunits

options.text: A unitary structure, since the centre can restructure the territory by law.
A confederal structure, since provinces are named in national law.
options.misconception: reads naming in national law as a confederation sign

options.text: A mixed regime, since provinces compete for national attention.
options.misconception: confuses territorial structure with regime classification

questions.explanation: A centre that can abolish provinces by ordinary legislation holds undivided legal authority, which is the unitary marker. Federalism would block such a change, and uniform rules appear in federal states as well.
questions.hint: Test whether the centre can abolish provinces.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the alternation test to a regime

stimulus.body: The extract notes that the founding election produced a working majority for one movement, and that in the three elections since, that movement has lost and returned to office without any period in which the opposition was barred. Election-day observers report that polling in the eastern districts was delayed but eventually completed.

questions.stem: Judged on the alternation test, what does this extract show about the country surveyed?

options.text: The country is authoritarian, because polling was delayed in the eastern districts.
options.misconception: treats any administrative delay as proof of authoritarianism

options.text: The country is a hybrid regime, because delays make every election unfair.
options.misconception: assumes a delay settles the question of electoral fairness

options.text: The country is democratic, because power has changed hands peacefully.
The country is federal, because different districts are treated differently.
options.misconception: reads differing regional conditions as a federal structure

questions.explanation: The alternation test asks whether power has changed hands peacefully, and the record shows the movement losing office and returning. Administrative delays do not by themselves defeat the test.
questions.hint: Ask whether rulers actually changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess executive accountability in a given design
questions.stem: Noor must write the handbook section comparing a presidency that answers to voters with a cabinet that answers to the chamber.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should contrast the two routes of accountability directly. A directly elected president claims a mandate from the whole electorate and is difficult to remove between elections, so the corrective mechanism is the ballot at the next scheduled vote. A cabinet that depends on legislative confidence can be removed much faster, at any point when the chamber loses tolerance, which makes the government more responsive between elections but also more vulnerable to short-lived coalitions and backroom bargaining. The trade the handbook should underline is that the frequency of correction is not the same as the strength of mandate.

questions.explanation: Presidential executives answer to voters at the next election; confidence-dependent cabinets can be removed at any time. One offers stability, the other speed of correction.
questions.hint: Compare who can remove the executive, and when.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits placed on devolved authority
questions.stem: In the survey host country, a regional assembly runs its own transport service, but a national act allows the centre to end the arrangement by ordinary statute.

options.text: This is delegation, because the centre keeps the right to withdraw.
This is devolution, because the region runs a service on its own authority.
options.misconception: confuses operational autonomy with transferred legal power

options.text: This is federalism, because two authorities handle transport.
options.misconception: mistakes shared administration for a federal division

options.text: This is a unitary system, because the national act can end anything.
options.misconception: assumes central power proves unitary state structure

questions.explanation: A regional body running a service under rules the centre may unilaterally end has been delegated to, not devolved. Devolution involves powers the centre gives up, and federalism would protect the region constitutionally.
questions.hint: Ask whether the centre can end it.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the trade-off in a mixed institutional design
questions.stem: A team leader asks why the survey host country pairs a fixed-term presidency with a confidence-dependent cabinet.

options.text: It creates two competing executives who may disagree on policy.
options.misconception: assumes two executives must disagree rather than cooperate

options.text: It combines a stable mandate with the ability to correct a failed cabinet.
It exists so that no single office can be held for more than one term.
options.misconception: invents a term limit that the arrangement does not state

options.text: It reflects a tradition of rotating leadership between the two offices.
options.misconception: explains the design by custom rather than its stated functions

questions.explanation: A fixed-term presidency supplies stability while a confidence-dependent cabinet supplies a route to correct a failed government. The design trades speed against continuity, not rival executives.
questions.hint: Weigh stability against correctability.

questions.learningObjective: Identify how federal disputes are resolved

stimulus.body: The note records a land dispute in which the valley council and the water authority each claimed jurisdiction over the upper catchment. The constitutional court held that both bodies had concurrent competence, and ordered a joint management plan. The court also warned that neither body may dissolve the other.

questions.stem: What does the case note indicate about the constitutional order of the country surveyed?

options.text: A unitary order, because a single court can settle any dispute.
options.misconception: assumes a single court implies a unitary constitution

options.text: A confederal order, because the two bodies keep separate identities.
options.misconception: reads separate identities as evidence of confederation

options.text: A federal order, because each body holds powers the other cannot remove.
A hybrid regime, because the authorities disagree about jurisdiction.
options.misconception: confuses a jurisdictional dispute with regime unfairness

questions.explanation: Concurrent constitutionally protected competence, and the warning that neither body may dissolve the other, indicate a federal order. A single court can exist in any structure, and institutional disagreement is not unfairness.
questions.hint: Look for powers each side cannot remove.

options.misconception: dismisses media bias as irrelevant to electoral fairness

options.misconception: treats any distortion as removing the hybrid category

options.text: The argument is sound, because hybrid status needs no unfairness at all.
options.misconception: invents an unfairness-free definition of hybrid regimes

options.text: The argument is weak, because real competition with systematic distortion is hybrid.

questions.explanation: Hybrid regimes combine real competition with systematic unfairness, so this distortion points to the hybrid label rather than authoritarian rule. Treating any distortion as total misreads the categories.
questions.hint: Weigh real competition against distortion.

stimulus.body: The field note describes a president elected directly for a six-year term who promulgates the laws passed by the assembly. It also describes a prime minister who chairs the council and must secure a confidence vote. Observers note that the president and the prime minister are usually from the same movement.

questions.stem: Which label for the arrangement in the field note is best supported?

options.text: A mixed system, because executive elements of both kinds are present.
A presidential system, because the head of state holds the longest mandate.
options.misconception: ranks executive elements by length of mandate

options.text: A parliamentary system, because the government depends on confidence.
options.misconception: ignores the elected presidency when naming the system

options.text: A hybrid regime, because the two offices belong to the same movement.
options.misconception: treats shared party affiliation as evidence of unfairness

questions.explanation: A directly elected presidency with real authority and a confidence-dependent cabinet are elements of two executive designs, so a mixed label fits. Their shared affiliation speaks to cooperation, not electoral unfairness.
questions.hint: Name the elements, then judge fairness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the confidence rule to government stability
questions.stem: Noor must explain in the survey handbook why a confidence vote is run by the legislature rather than by a party's own members.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that the confidence rule is a check located outside the government and outside the party that supports it. If a party's own members decided whether to sustain a cabinet, the government would be answerable only to itself, and a disagreement over a budget or a scandal could never produce a government that actually leaves office. Placing the test in the legislature gives opposition parties a route to force accountability, at the cost of making the government's life depend on shifting majorities and on the bargaining that surrounds them.

questions.explanation: Putting the test in the legislature places accountability outside the government itself. That lets opponents force a government's departure, at the cost of dependence on shifting majorities.
questions.hint: Ask where the check sits.

options.misconception: confuses the threshold with a constituency test

options.misconception: attaches thresholds to a particular state structure

The sixth party is included, because proportional allocation ignores thresholds.
options.misconception: ignores the threshold rule when allocating seats

questions.explanation: A legal threshold excludes parties below a stated vote share, so the sixth party gains no seats despite polling three percent. Thresholds belong to proportional allocation generally, not to any state structure.
questions.hint: Apply the threshold rule directly.

options.misconception: infers confederation from the method of choosing the centre

options.misconception: reads subunit legislatures as evidence of regime unfairness

questions.stem: Another surveyor argues that a regime whose incumbent party has never lost an election in fifty years cannot be democratic.

The argument fails, because long incumbency can reflect popular satisfaction.
options.misconception: treats popularity as evidence against long incumbency

options.misconception: misplaces the alternation test at the district level

options.text: The argument holds, because democratic systems require frequent turnover.
options.misconception: adds a turnover requirement the test does not contain

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess executive accountability in a given design
questions.stem: Ana must compare in the handbook how two governments are held to account when a minister fails to deliver a promised reform.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should separate the two mechanisms clearly. A confidence system places the answerability for a failed minister with the legislature, which can question the minister, refuse to pass a budget or bring down the whole cabinet quickly, so the correction arrives well before the next scheduled election. A presidential system disperses correction into two channels, since the minister's own president may dismiss him, but the president himself remains answerable only at the ballot box. The first mechanism is faster and more exposed to coalition bargaining, while the second is slower but harder for a failed administration to escape.

questions.explanation: Confidence systems let the legislature correct a failing government between elections. Presidential systems route correction through the executive and then to voters at the next ballot.
questions.hint: Compare speed and route of correction.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits placed on devolved authority
questions.stem: In the host country, the devolved body sets its own rules for land use, yet a national court may strike them down as ultra vires.

options.text: This is delegation, because the centre's courts still control the region.
options.misconception: equates judicial review with the absence of transferred power

options.text: This is federalism, because a court can void regional legislation.
options.misconception: mistakes judicial review for a constitutional division of powers

options.text: This is devolution with a legal limit, because the region sets its own rules.
This is a unitary system, because national courts stand above all rules.
options.misconception: confuses the place of a court with the structure of the state

questions.explanation: A devolved body making its own rules is genuine devolution, and judicial review limits that power rather than proving delegation. Federalism concerns the constitutional distribution of authority, not the existence of a court.
questions.hint: A limit on devolution is still devolution.

options.misconception: reads a cabinet question as a question of state structure

options.text: A trade-off between a durable mandate and the ability to correct a cabinet.

questions.explanation: The fixed presidential mandate offers continuity while the confidence rule offers a way to dismiss a cabinet that fails. This is a trade-off between durability of mandate and speed of correction, not a federal question.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the confidence rule to government stability
questions.stem: Noor must write in the handbook why a no-confidence vote is often described as a blunt instrument in parliamentary systems.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that a confidence vote is blunt because it does not evaluate any part of the government's programme separately. If a single minister loses the support of a whole parliamentary group, the constitution may still require the entire cabinet to resign, so an opposition that holds a narrow majority can remove a government that retains majority support on most policies. The instrument is therefore powerful and quick, which is why governments pay close attention to internal party discipline, and why some constitutions add mechanisms that allow a single policy to be disapproved without bringing the whole cabinet down.

questions.explanation: A confidence vote judges the whole government, so a narrow majority can remove a cabinet still supported by most policy groups. That bluntness is why governments guard every party's support.
questions.hint: Think about what the vote covers.

questions.learningObjective: Assess executive accountability in a given design
questions.stem: A reviewer claims that a president who cannot be removed between elections is unaccountable in any sense.

options.text: The claim holds, because no check on a president is ever possible.
options.misconception: assumes no institutional check can exist on a president

options.text: The claim holds, because voters can only act at the next election.
options.misconception: confuses one removal route with the whole of accountability

options.text: The claim fails, because presidential systems are never democratic at all.
options.misconception: dismisses every presidential system as undemocratic

options.text: The claim overstates, because courts, legislatures and voters still act.

questions.explanation: A fixed term narrows the routes to removal but does not remove accountability, since courts, legislatures and the ballot box still act. The claim also ignores that many presidential systems are democracies.
questions.hint: Count the routes to correction, not one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits placed on devolved authority
questions.stem: The handbook must explain why devolved bodies are often given only defined fields of power rather than general powers.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that defined fields, called enumerated or residual powers, keep the devolved body's legal authority bounded and legible. If a region received general legislative power, the centre would need a principle for pulling back, and every disagreement would turn into a fight about sovereignty, whereas a list of subjects lets the centre see exactly what remains with it and what has moved. The same clarity helps disputes, because a conflict can be settled by asking which list an activity falls under rather than by measuring the strength of a claim.

questions.explanation: Defined fields keep the transferred authority bounded and make residual powers clear. General powers would leave every disagreement as a fight about sovereignty rather than a list question.
questions.hint: Ask what the centre keeps by implication.

options.misconception: reads negotiated agreement as evidence of confederation

Disputes are settled by the provinces alone, indicating a federal structure.
options.misconception: ignores the binding role of the centre in the settlement

questions.explanation: A centre that can make a scheme binding on provinces exercises superior authority, the unitary pattern, even though it negotiated rather than commanded. Confederation leaves the final say with provinces.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the features of a mixed system
questions.stem: Ana must set out in the handbook how a survey country with both an elected presidency and a confidence rule decides who actually governs.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that a mixed design usually splits the work in two. The presidency supplies the state's outward authority, representing the country in treaties, appointing the prime minister and often promulgating the laws the assembly passes, and it carries the mandate of the national election. The cabinet supplies the working government, administering policy, defending its programme in the assembly and surviving only while the assembly tolerates it. Which office dominates depends on the specific constitution and on the convention that has grown up around it, which is why two mixed systems can behave quite differently in practice.

questions.explanation: The presidency normally supplies the outward mandate and the cabinet the working government, with the balance set by constitution and convention. Two mixed systems can therefore behave very differently.
questions.hint: Look at who represents and who governs.

options.misconception: mistakes a voting threshold for a coalition requirement

questions.explanation: A no-confidence vote is a confidence rule, and this one adds a defined threshold of an absolute majority. That procedural detail does not turn the system into a presidential or a coalition arrangement.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits placed on devolved authority
questions.stem: The handbook must explain in what sense a devolved power remains a power of the centre that has been lent rather than given away.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that devolved authority is usually described as lent because the legal source of the power remains the centre. The enabling legislation states what has been transferred and on what conditions, and the centre keeps the theoretical capacity to legislate again, which is why scholars often say the arrangement rests on statute rather than on entrenched constitutional guarantees. Practically, a government may promise not to use that capacity, so the real limit is political as much as legal, and the arrangement can shift in either direction depending on what the centre is willing to do.

questions.explanation: Devolved powers stay legally rooted in the centre's enabling statute, so they are lent rather than given away. The real limit is often political, resting on what the centre is willing to use.
questions.hint: Ask where the legal source still sits.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the confidence rule to government stability
questions.stem: Ana must contrast in the handbook the parliamentary confidence rule with a presidential impeachment procedure.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should note that the two procedures aim at different things and use different tests. The confidence vote asks a simple question, whether the legislature still supports the government as a whole, and it is normally available at any time, so it is fast, binary and easy for an opposition to use. Impeachment asks whether specified serious misconduct has been proved, so it is slower, needs a defined standard and evidence, and usually ends in removal or acquittal rather than a change of government. The first corrects failing governments, the second punishes individuals, and confusing them obscures what accountability each mechanism can deliver.

questions.explanation: Confidence asks whether support continues and acts fast. Impeachment tests misconduct against a standard, so it is slower and aimed at individuals rather than at governments.
questions.hint: Separate removal of support from proof of wrongdoing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess executive accountability in a given design
questions.stem: Another handbook section must explain why the same office can be highly accountable in one country and weakly accountable in another.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that accountability is not a property of the office but of the whole structure around it. A president may be checked by a court that can strike down unlawful acts, by a legislature that can withhold appropriations, by an auditor with the power to publish findings, and by voters at the next election, and if several of those checks exist and work, the office is strongly accountable even with a long term. Where a constitution concentrates power, where an audit office reports only to the executive, or where the electoral competition is weak, the same title carries far less accountability.

questions.explanation: Accountability comes from the checks around an office, not its title. Courts, legislatures, auditors and the ballot box each add accountability only if they can actually act.
questions.hint: Look at who can check the office.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish federal from unitary authority
questions.stem: A field handbook states that in a unitary state all legal authority rests in the national centre and local bodies exist only where the centre creates them.

options.text: That is the federal marker, since local bodies are constitutionally created.
options.misconception: reverses the unitary and federal descriptions

options.text: That is the confederal marker, since the centre is created by the units.
options.misconception: invents a creation story that reverses who founds whom

options.text: That is the hybrid marker, since local bodies compete with the centre.
options.misconception: reads administrative structure as a regime classification

options.text: That is the unitary marker, since subunits stand at the centre's pleasure.

questions.explanation: Local bodies existing only where the centre creates them, with all authority legally resting above them, is the unitary marker. Federalism would protect subunits against such central control.
questions.hint: Ask where subunits stand legally.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the alternation test to a regime

stimulus.body: The case file describes an opposition that won a plurality in every district of the country but never a majority of seats, and that has contested every election without being barred. Analysts note that the governing party has changed twice in the last decade, once after a transfer of support between two of its own factions.

questions.stem: What does the case file indicate about the surveyed country?

options.text: The country shows a democratic pattern of contest, though the government changed hands.
The country is authoritarian, because the opposition never won seats.
options.misconception: treats an opposition's seat weakness as authoritarianism

options.text: The country is democratic, because every election was contested.
options.misconception: treats the presence of contests as the whole democratic test

options.text: The country is federal, because districts are decisive in the result.
options.misconception: reads the role of districts as evidence of federal structure

questions.explanation: Contested elections, no bars on candidates and changes of government point to a democratic pattern, even though the opposition converted votes into seats poorly. That reflects the electoral rule.
questions.hint: Weigh contest against seat conversion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess executive accountability in a given design
questions.stem: A further surveyor argues that a government which can be removed by the legislature is always more accountable than a president elected by the people.

options.text: The claim holds, because the legislature is a single checkable body.
options.misconception: assumes one check always outweighs any number of others

options.text: The claim overstates, because accountability depends on the whole structure.
The claim holds, because elections cannot discipline any executive.
options.misconception: ignores the discipline provided by the ballot box

options.text: The claim overstates, because elected presidents face no legal limits.
options.misconception: assumes an elected executive is free of legal constraints

questions.explanation: Accountability rests on the number and strength of checks around an office, so a removable cabinet and an elected president cannot be ranked without knowing courts, auditors and the contest.
questions.hint: Ask what other checks exist.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits placed on devolved authority
questions.stem: The handbook must explain how devolution can be widened or narrowed without a new constitution being written.

answer.exemplar: The handbook should explain that devolved powers are usually set by ordinary legislation, so they can be widened or narrowed in the same way they were granted, through a statute of the national legislature. This is what makes devolution flexible and also what makes it contingent, since a future majority may legislate the arrangement away, which is why devolution is often contrasted with the entrenched constitutional division of a federal state. The handbook should add that governments often treat the arrangement as settled by convention and hesitate to unwind it, so the legal possibility and the practical expectation can pull in different directions.

questions.explanation: Devolved powers rest on ordinary statute, so they can be widened or narrowed legislatively. That flexibility distinguishes devolution from an entrenched federal division, and makes it contingent.
questions.hint: Ask what instrument carries the power.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the trade-off in a mixed institutional design

stimulus.body: The closing note records that the surveyed country adopted a fixed presidential term after a series of unstable cabinets, and that the confidence rule was left untouched. Officials report that cabinets now last longer, while the number of no-confidence votes in the last decade has been low. The author asks what the change achieved.

questions.stem: What does the closing note indicate about the mixed design in the surveyed country?

options.text: It produced a hybrid regime, because cabinets became longer-serving.
options.misconception: confuses longer cabinet terms with the hybrid regime category

options.text: It removed electoral fairness, because the presidency now dominates.
options.misconception: assumes a dominant presidency proves electoral unfairness

options.text: It restored pure parliamentary accountability, because the confidence rule survived.
options.misconception: claims a surviving confidence rule restores a pure system

options.text: It traded speed of correction for continuity in leadership.

questions.explanation: Fixing the presidential term was aimed at stability, and longer cabinets with few confidence votes show the continuity side of the trade-off. Nothing in the note indicates a change in electoral fairness.
questions.hint: Read the outcome the note reports.
